newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Rotterdam port set to expand seawards.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rotterdam port set to expand seawards.

text.p: The Dutch, masters of land reclamation, plan to push the sea back again.
But a scheme to extend the port of Rotterdam has run up against spirited opposition from environmental groups.
The government will soon decide whether to extend the port by up to 20 percent of its land area.
It now ends at a piece of reclaimed land called the Maasvlakte. The new addition would be called Maasvlakte Twee (Two) and work would begin in 1999.
The Port of Rotterdam authority has urged the expansion for some time and debate has been lively among local residents, industrialists and ecologists.
Rotterdam says it is almost at bursting point and needs to expand to remain the world's largest port in tonnage terms.
"In the existing port area, we have 200 hectares (500 acres) left for new companies," said spokesman Rob van Dijk.
At current rates of growth, he says, capacity would be reached in two more years.
Environmentalists counter that the port authority should begin by using its current land area more efficiently.
"They want to be the biggest port. They should aim instead at being the fastest, the smartest and the cleanest," said Arno Steekelenburg of Dutch environmental group Milieu Federatie.
The final report, on which the government will base its decision, is due shortly.
"The report has to be finalised, but it is very close," said Hans Scholten of the Ministry of Transport and Waterways.
GOVERNMENT REPORT

An initial government-inspired report, published earlier this year, said that by 2020 Rotterdam needed another 700-1,000 hectares (1,730-2,471 acres) to keep up with growth in container traffic and in the distribution and petrochemical sectors. Without expansion, some business would go elsewhere, it concluded.
"As far as deep-sea container traffic is concerned, it seems foreign ports would be the only option," the report said.
The two leading proposals steer a simple course between wishes of the environmentalists -- no expansion -- and those of the Port Authority to expand by 2,000 hectares (4,942 acres).
The Maasvlakte Twee will either be a 500 hectare (1,235-acre) block of land or a harbour of 1,000 hectares, an increase in the port area of 10 or 20 percent.
The cost estimates range from two billion to 6.5 billion guilders ($3.3 billion).
A mooted nature and recreation area, aimed at appeasing environmental groups and locals could add a further one billion guilders.
The proximity of the final decision has fuelled the debate.
Environmentalists have questioned the assumption that the expansion would have any economic benefits for the local area.
PROS AND CONS
Rotterdam's unemployment, at 16 percent, is twice the national average but Milieu Federatie and other environmental groups say port activities have become steadily less labour intensive.
An expansion would bring little economic benefit, but rising pollution, they say, as more container trucks rumble towards Rotterdam. They believe their argument is winning support.
"Children living within a kilometre (mile) of roads heavy with cargo traffic have severe lung problems. A Maasvlakte Twee could bring an extra 45,000 lorries per day," Steekelenburg said.
He said the port authority had made no progress in increasing the use of pipelines and inland barges.

The authority appears to have accepted the two leading proposals. The more modest expansion plans should still allow Rotterdam to challenge for position with the world's largest container ports, Singapore and Hong Kong.
However, it remains concerned as to who should pay. Although it would control the new land, it says the benefits would really be for the Dutch nation as a whole.
"The Dutch government should pay 70 to 80 percent, we think," said Van Dijk.
